title: Angular momentum and rotational kinetic energy
summary: A spinning body has [[angular-momentum|angular momentum]], $L = I\omega$. With no resultant external [[torque|torque]] it stays constant, so a spinning body that pulls its mass towards the axis speeds up. Spinning also stores [[rotational-kinetic-energy|rotational kinetic energy]], $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$.

goals.text: Calculate the angular momentum of a rotating body with $L = I\omega$.
Use $\Delta L = \tau\Delta t = \Delta(I\omega)$, including the area under a torque–time graph.
Apply [[conservation-of-angular-momentum|conservation of angular momentum]] when a body changes shape or two bodies start turning together.
Calculate rotational kinetic energy with $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ or $\frac{L^{2}}{2I}$, including for a body rolling without slipping.
Explain why [[kinetic-energy|kinetic energy]] can change while angular momentum stays constant.

before.prompt: A constant resultant [[force|force]] of $\pu{30 N}$ acts on a trolley for $\pu{0.40 s}$. What is the change in the trolley's [[linear-momentum|linear momentum]], in N s?
before.hint: The [[impulse|impulse]] of a constant resultant force is $F\Delta t$, and it equals the change in momentum.
before.explain: $\Delta p = F\Delta t = 30 \times 0.40 = \pu{12 N s}$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.6}}.

before.prompt: Two small $\pu{0.50 kg}$ masses sit on a light rod, each $\pu{0.20 m}$ from the axis of rotation. Calculate the [[moment-of-inertia|moment of inertia]] of the pair about that axis, in kg m². Give 2 significant figures.
before.hint: Use $I = \sum mr^{2}$: add $mr^{2}$ for each mass.

before.prompt: A $\pu{0.20 kg}$ ball moves at $\pu{6.0 m s-1}$. Calculate its [[kinetic-energy|kinetic energy]], in J. Give 2 significant figures.

blocks.text: A heavy spinning wheel is hard to stop, as a heavy moving trolley is. For the trolley, this is measured by linear momentum, $p = mv$.
For rotation, swap each linear quantity for its turning partner. Mass $m$ becomes moment of inertia $I$, and speed $v$ becomes angular speed $\omega$. The product is angular momentum.

blocks.statement: The angular momentum of a body rotating about an axis is $L = I\omega$, where $I$ is its moment of inertia about that axis and $\omega$ is its angular speed. Unit: $\text{kg m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
blocks.plain: How much rotational motion a spinning body has.

blocks.text: This equation, and the others in this lesson, are in section A.4 of the data booklet. $\omega$ must be in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$: one revolution is $2\pi$ rad.
You don't need its vector direction, but give its sense (clockwise or anticlockwise) when bodies turn opposite ways.

blocks.question: A potter's wheel has a moment of inertia of $\pu{0.85 kg m2}$ about its axle. It turns at 2.4 revolutions per second. Calculate its angular momentum.
steps: Convert to rad s⁻¹. Each revolution is $2\pi$ rad, so $\omega = 2\pi \times 2.4 = 15.08\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.
The data have 2 significant figures, so round to 2.

blocks.text: Using revolutions per second as $\omega$. Multiply by $2\pi$ to get $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ first.

blocks.question: Two small $\pu{0.30 kg}$ masses are fixed to a light rod, one on each side of the axis and each $\pu{0.45 m}$ from it. The rod turns at $\pu{6.0 rad s-1}$. Calculate the angular momentum of the system.
steps: Moment of inertia: the rod is light, so only the masses count. $I = \sum mr^{2} = 2 \times 0.30 \times 0.45^{2} = \pu{0.1215 kg m2}$.

blocks.prompt: A thin ring and a uniform disc have the same mass and radius. Both spin about their central axes at the same angular speed. Which has the larger angular momentum?
blocks.hint: Same $\omega$, so compare $I$. Where is each body's mass?
blocks.explain: All the ring's mass is at the full radius, but much of the disc's is nearer the axis. So the ring has the larger $I$, and with equal $\omega$, the larger $L = I\omega$.

blocks.prompt: A bicycle wheel with moment of inertia $\pu{0.12 kg m2}$ spins at $\pu{25 rad s-1}$. Calculate its angular momentum, in kg m² s⁻¹. Give 2 significant figures.
blocks.hint: $L = I\omega$; $\omega$ is already in rad s⁻¹.

blocks.text: A force acting for a time gives a body an [[impulse|impulse]], $F\Delta t$, which equals its change in linear momentum. Turning works the same way: a resultant torque acting for a time changes the angular momentum.

blocks.statement: A resultant torque $\tau$ acting for a time $\Delta t$ gives an angular impulse $\tau\Delta t$. It equals the change in angular momentum: $\Delta L = \tau\Delta t = \Delta(I\omega)$.
blocks.why: From {{lesson:1.13}}, $\tau = I\alpha = I\frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}$ for a rigid body, so $\tau\Delta t = I\Delta\omega = \Delta(I\omega)$.

blocks.text: Angular impulse has the unit N m s, which is the same as $\text{kg m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. Rearranged, $\tau = \frac{\Delta L}{\Delta t}$: the resultant torque is the rate of change of angular momentum.
Signs matter here. Take the direction of rotation as positive. A torque that slows the body is then negative, and so is its angular impulse.

blocks.question: A grinding wheel with moment of inertia $\pu{0.024 kg m2}$ starts from rest. Its motor applies a constant resultant torque of $\pu{0.65 N m}$ for $\pu{2.5 s}$. Calculate the wheel's final angular speed.
steps: Angular impulse: $\tau\Delta t = 0.65 \times 2.5 = \pu{1.625 N m s}$.
This equals $\Delta L = I\omega_\text{f} - I\omega_\text{i}$, and $\omega_\text{i} = 0$, so $0.024\,\omega_\text{f} = 1.625$.

blocks.text: When the resultant torque varies, the area under a torque–time graph is the angular impulse, just as the area under a force–time graph is the impulse.

blocks.alt: Graph of resultant torque in newton metres against time in seconds for a rotor. The torque rises in a straight line from zero at time zero to 4.0 newton metres at 0.50 seconds, stays at 4.0 newton metres until 1.50 seconds, then falls in a straight line to zero at 2.00 seconds. The shaded area under the graph is labelled angular impulse.
blocks.caption: The area under a torque–time graph is the angular impulse, $\Delta L$.

blocks.question: A rotor with moment of inertia $\pu{0.15 kg m2}$ is spinning at $\pu{12 rad s-1}$. A motor then applies the resultant torque in the figure, in the direction of rotation. Determine the rotor's angular speed at $t = \pu{2.00 s}$.
steps: Split the area into two triangles and a rectangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times 0.50 \times 4.0 + 1.00 \times 4.0 + \frac{1}{2} \times 0.50 \times 4.0 = \pu{6.0 N m s}$.
So $\Delta L = \pu{6.0 N m s}$, and $\Delta\omega = \frac{\Delta L}{I} = \frac{6.0}{0.15} = 40\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.
The torque acts in the direction of rotation, so the rotor speeds up: $\omega = 12 + 40 = 52\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.

blocks.prompt: What does the area under a graph of resultant torque against time give?
blocks.hint: Torque × time is an angular impulse.

options.text: the work done by the torque

blocks.explain: Area = $\tau\Delta t$ = angular impulse = $\Delta L$. To get $\Delta\omega$ you still divide by $I$. Work done by a torque depends on the angle turned, not the time.

blocks.prompt: A wheel with moment of inertia $\pu{0.40 kg m2}$ slows from $\pu{30 rad s-1}$ to $\pu{18 rad s-1}$ in $\pu{4.0 s}$. Taking the direction of rotation as positive, calculate the average resultant torque, in N m. Give 2 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Find $\Delta L = I(\omega_\text{f} - \omega_\text{i})$ first, then divide by the time. Watch the sign.
blocks.explain: $\Delta L = 0.40 \times (18 - 30) = -4.8\ \text{N m s}$, so $\tau = \frac{-4.8}{4.0} = -1.2\ \text{N m}$. The minus sign shows the torque opposes the rotation.

blocks.text: If no resultant torque acts, $\tau\Delta t = 0$, so $\Delta L = 0$. The angular momentum can't change.

blocks.statement: The total angular momentum of a system stays constant unless a resultant external torque acts on it.
blocks.plain: Without an outside twist, a system's spin can't change.

blocks.text: Torques between parts of the system are internal. They come in equal and opposite pairs, so they move angular momentum from one part to another without changing the total.
A force through the axis has no torque about it. A force parallel to the axis, like the weight of a body turning about a vertical axis, has none either.

blocks.statement: With no resultant external torque, $I_{1}\omega_{1} = I_{2}\omega_{2}$. If the moment of inertia decreases, the angular speed increases in the same ratio.
blocks.why: $L = I\omega$ is constant, so $I$ and $\omega$ are inversely proportional.

blocks.alt: Two views from above of a student on a stool that turns freely about a vertical axis through its centre. On the left she holds a dumbbell in each hand with her arms stretched out, so the dumbbells are far from the axis; a short curved arrow shows slow anticlockwise rotation, labelled I large, omega small. On the right she has pulled the dumbbells in to her chest, close to the axis; a longer curved arrow shows faster anticlockwise rotation, labelled I small, omega large. Between the panels a note reads L equals I omega, the same in both.
blocks.caption: Pulling mass towards the axis lowers $I$, so $\omega$ rises and $L = I\omega$ stays the same.

blocks.question: A student sits on a stool that turns freely about a vertical axis. With dumbbells held at arm's length, her moment of inertia (with the stool) is $\pu{3.6 kg m2}$ and she turns at $\pu{2.0 rad s-1}$. She pulls the dumbbells in, and her moment of inertia falls to $\pu{1.5 kg m2}$. Calculate her new angular speed.
steps: The stool turns freely, so there is no resultant external torque about the axis. Angular momentum is conserved.
$\omega_{2} = \frac{7.2}{1.5} = 4.8\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. $I$ fell, so $\omega$ rose, as expected.

blocks.question: Explain why the student's angular speed increases when she pulls the dumbbells in.
steps: Say why angular momentum is conserved.
Say what happens to the moment of inertia, and why.
Use $L = I\omega$ to conclude.
blocks.answer: The stool turns freely, so there is no resultant external torque on the student, dumbbells and stool. So their total angular momentum $L = I\omega$ stays constant. Pulling the dumbbells in moves mass closer to the axis, so her moment of inertia decreases. For $I\omega$ to stay constant, her angular speed must increase.

verify.truth: no resultant external torque so angular momentum conserved; mass moves closer to the axis so moment of inertia decreases; L = I omega constant so omega increases

blocks.text: Conservation also links coupled bodies. When two bodies on the same axis grip each other, friction between them is internal. Each body's angular momentum changes, but their total does not.

blocks.question: A turntable with moment of inertia $\pu{0.020 kg m2}$ spins freely at $\pu{3.5 rad s-1}$. A ring with moment of inertia $\pu{0.0060 kg m2}$, not rotating, is dropped centrally onto it. Friction between them soon makes them turn together. Calculate their final angular speed.
steps: The turntable spins freely and the friction between ring and turntable is internal, so the total angular momentum is conserved.
After, they share one $\omega$, with $I = 0.020 + 0.0060 = \pu{0.026 kg m2}$.

blocks.prompt: A playground roundabout spins freely. A child, standing still on the ground, steps straight onto its edge. What happens to the roundabout's angular speed?
blocks.hint: The child adds mass far from the axis, but brings no angular momentum.
blocks.explain: The total $L$ is unchanged, but the child increases $I$. So $\omega = \frac{L}{I}$ decreases.

blocks.prompt: A diver leaves the board turning at $\pu{1.8 rad s-1}$, with a moment of inertia of $\pu{9.0 kg m2}$ about her centre of mass. In the air she tucks, and it falls to $\pu{3.6 kg m2}$. Calculate her new angular speed, in rad s⁻¹. Give 2 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Her weight acts at her centre of mass, so it has no torque about it. Use $I_{1}\omega_{1} = I_{2}\omega_{2}$.

blocks.text: A spinning flywheel can stay in one place, yet every part of it is moving. So it has kinetic energy, stored in its rotation.

blocks.statement: The rotational kinetic energy of a body turning about an axis is $E_\text{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$, where $I$ is its moment of inertia about that axis. Unit: J.
blocks.plain: The energy a body has because it is spinning.

blocks.text: Why $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$? A small mass $m$ at distance $r$ moves at $v = \omega r$, so its energy is $\frac{1}{2}mr^{2}\omega^{2}$. Adding these over the body gives $\frac{1}{2}(\sum mr^{2})\omega^{2} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$.
The second form comes from putting $\omega = \frac{L}{I}$ into the first. Use it when you know $L$.

blocks.question: A roundabout has a moment of inertia of $\pu{240 kg m2}$ and turns at $\pu{1.50 rad s-1}$. Calculate its rotational kinetic energy.
steps: $E_\text{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 240 \times 1.50^{2} = \pu{270 J}$, to 3 significant figures.
Check with the other form: $L = 240 \times 1.50 = 360\ \text{kg m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$, and $\frac{L^{2}}{2I} = \frac{360^{2}}{480} = \pu{270 J}$.

blocks.text: Angular momentum can be conserved while kinetic energy is not. Look again at the student on the stool.

blocks.question: For the student on the stool, $I$ fell from $\pu{3.6 kg m2}$ to $\pu{1.5 kg m2}$ while $L$ stayed at $7.2\ \text{kg m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. Determine the change in her rotational kinetic energy.
steps: Before: $E_\text{k} = \frac{L^{2}}{2I} = \frac{7.2^{2}}{2 \times 3.6} = \pu{7.2 J}$.
After: $E_\text{k} = \frac{7.2^{2}}{2 \times 1.5} = \pu{17.28 J}$. Use the new $I$ here, not the old one.
Change: $17.28 - 7.2 = +10.08\ \text{J}$. It is positive, so the energy increases.
The extra energy comes from the work her arm muscles do pulling the dumbbells inwards.

blocks.text: Using the same moment of inertia before and after a change of shape. $I$ changes, so work out each energy with its own $I$ and $\omega$.
Coupled bodies go the other way. When the ring grips the turntable, friction turns some kinetic energy into internal energy, as in an inelastic collision.
A rolling wheel both moves along and spins. Rolling without slipping means the contact point does not slide, so $v = \omega R$, where $v$ is the speed of the centre and $R$ the radius.

blocks.statement: For a body rolling without slipping, total kinetic energy = translational + rotational = $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$, with $v = \omega R$.
blocks.why: For the moving-along part, the body's mass is treated as concentrated at its [[centre-of-mass|centre of mass]]; the spinning part is about an axis through that point.

blocks.question: A uniform solid cylinder, $\pu{1.8 kg}$ and $\pu{0.050 m}$ in radius, starts at rest at the top of a ramp. It rolls down without slipping, through a vertical drop of $\pu{0.60 m}$. Its moment of inertia is $\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$. Determine its speed at the bottom.
steps: The contact point does not slide, so friction does no work. With air resistance negligible, the lost gravitational potential energy all becomes kinetic energy.
With $\omega = \frac{v}{R}$, the rotational part is $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}MR^{2} \times \frac{v^{2}}{R^{2}} = \frac{1}{4}Mv^{2}$.
So $Mgh = \frac{1}{2}Mv^{2} + \frac{1}{4}Mv^{2} = \frac{3}{4}Mv^{2}$. $M$ and $R$ cancel.
$v = \sqrt{\frac{4gh}{3}} = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 9.8 \times 0.60}{3}} = 2.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, using $g = \pu{9.8 m s-2}$ from the data booklet.
A frictionless sliding block would reach $\sqrt{2gh} = \pu{3.4 m s-1}$. The cylinder is slower: a third of its energy is rotational.

blocks.prompt: The angular speed of a flywheel doubles. What happens to its rotational kinetic energy?

options.text: it becomes four times as large

blocks.explain: $E_\text{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ with $I$ unchanged, so doubling $\omega$ multiplies $E_\text{k}$ by $2^{2} = 4$.

verify.truth: it becomes four times as large

blocks.prompt: A turntable ($I = \pu{0.020 kg m2}$) spinning at $\pu{3.5 rad s-1}$ is joined by a non-rotating ring ($I = \pu{0.0060 kg m2}$), and they end up turning together at the same angular speed. Calculate the kinetic energy lost, in J. Give 2 significant figures.
blocks.hint: First find the shared $\omega$ from conservation of $L$. Then compare $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ before and after, each with its own $I$.
blocks.explain: Before: $\frac{1}{2} \times 0.020 \times 3.5^{2} = \pu{0.1225 J}$. After: $\frac{L^{2}}{2I} = \frac{0.070^{2}}{2 \times 0.026} = \pu{0.0942 J}$. Lost: $\pu{0.028 J}$, to internal energy through friction.

blocks.text: With no resultant external torque, angular momentum is conserved: $I_{1}\omega_{1} = I_{2}\omega_{2}$. Lower $I$ means higher $\omega$.
The area under a resultant torque–time graph is the angular impulse, $\Delta L$. Units: N m s = $\text{kg m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$; $\omega$ in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$.
Conserved $L$ does not mean conserved kinetic energy: pulling mass inwards raises $E_\text{k}$; coupling two bodies that turn at different rates lowers it.
Rolling without slipping: $v = \omega R$, and total $E_\text{k} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$.

mistakes: Claiming angular momentum is conserved without saying why. State that no resultant external torque acts on the system.
Assuming kinetic energy is conserved because angular momentum is. Work out $E_\text{k}$ before and after, each with its own $I$.
Leaving $\omega$ in revolutions per second or per minute. Convert to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ before using $L = I\omega$ or $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$.
Forgetting the rotational energy of a rolling body. Its total kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$.
Reading the area under a torque–time graph as a change in angular speed. It is $\Delta L$; divide by $I$.
examTips: "Explain" a change in angular speed with three points: no resultant external torque, so $L$ is constant; why $I$ changes; so $\omega$ changes inversely.
In "determine" questions, write the conservation equation $I_{1}\omega_{1} = I_{2}\omega_{2}$ before substituting. Give $\omega$ in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ and $L$ in $\text{kg m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
In Paper 1A ratio questions, pick the form that holds one quantity fixed: $\frac{L^{2}}{2I}$ when $L$ is the same, $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ when $\omega$ is.
In "show that" rolling questions, write the energy equation with both kinetic terms, substitute $\omega = \frac{v}{R}$, and give one more significant figure than the stated value.
